newsitem.title: USA: AIDS researchers studying two-drug regimen.
newsitem.headline: AIDS researchers studying two-drug regimen.

text.p: AIDS researchers who made a breakthrough by combining three drugs into a highly effective "cocktail" treatment are now looking at a two-drug mix they say could be an even more potent attack on the virus.
Unlike the three-drug cocktail, which works by striking the virus at different junctures in its replication process, the two-drug treatment combines two brands of the same drug, a protease inhibitor.

Protease inhibitors are already a cornerstone of virtually all aggressive AIDS treatments, but only recently have researchers begun to look at exploiting the subtle differences between different brands of the drug. Currently Abbott Laboratories Inc, Merck and Co Inc. and Roche Holding Ltd's Hoffman-La Roche division all make protease inhibitors, which perform the same basic function but have subtle variations.

Those companies and others have been testing different combinations of brands and will report their findings at the Fourth Annual Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections, a leading forum for AIDS research, in Washington this week.

"Protease inhibitors all work by the same general mechanism but they do so in slightly different ways," said Peter Johnson, president of San Diego-based Agouron Pharmaceuticals Inc., which has a protease inhibitor awaiting approval by the Food and Drug Administration.
"One (drug) may continue to work after another has failed. The enemy to drugs is the diseases' resistance," Johnson said.
Initial studies into this theory have been encouraging. Last November, Abbott and Hoffman-La Roche said the combination of their two drugs drove down viral load by more than 99.9 percent.
Even that rate of success is not a cure, Dr. Charles Farthing, medical director of AIDS Healthcare Foundation in Los Angeles, which was one site of the study, told Reuters.

"Not when you're starting with many, many millions of virus particles," he said. But he agreed it offered hope to patients who have failed with the three-drug therapy and to those sensitive to the side effects of that regimen.
Protease inhibitors work by blocking the virus from leaving a patient's DNA and invading the rest of the body.

The prevailing three-drug treatment combines one protease inhibitor with two "transcriptate inhibitors" such as AZT or 3TC, which attack the virus at an earlier stage in the process by which it spreads. But because the HIV virus is prone to mutations that make it hightly resistant, two drugs that attack it at the same time might be the most effective means of suppressing it, many researchers believe.

"You want to hit the virus as hard as you can at once, don't let it have too many opportunities to escape," said Mehta and Isaly analyst Edmund Debler, who follows some of the small drug companies like Agouron that are trying to bring new protease inhibitors onto the market.

Encouraged by early tests of the two-drug combination, companies like Agouron and Vertex believe the market will be large enough to support more than the three protease inhibitors already on the market.

"If the data holds the two-drug therapy could stand to challenge the three-drug treatment," Agouron President Peter Johnson told a recent investor conference. "We could be well on our way to seeing a new paradigm for HIV treatment."
